The more excellent an art is, the fewer practitioners it has, and the more critics. Because of its loftiness, it is not for everyone to climb. **Plato** seems to have judged no art among all to be more noble than **Astrology** <term>Astrology: in this period, the term "astrologia" encompassed both the scientific mapping of the stars (astronomy) and the study of their influence on human affairs</term>, since he said that eyes were given to humans primarily for the sake of this art. He evidently understood the same thing that **Saint Paul** <note>original: "D. Paulus" (Divus Paulus). This refers to the biblical argument in Romans 1:20 that the creator's nature is revealed through the physical world.</note> wrote: that the minds of men, by looking at the heavens, arrive at the knowledge of God through the contemplation of His most beautiful work, as if by a shortcut. But who would dare to convince themselves that they have intimately understood the nature and all the inner secrets of this immense and inaccessible heaven, which is the subject of **Astrologers**? Even those things that crawl upon the earth, are handled by our hands, and trodden by our feet, have been explored—as far as their natural composition and essence are concerned—by the wisest **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to "Natural Philosophers," the historical term for those who studied the physical sciences and the nature of reality.</note> in such a way that they left behind mostly doubt and falsehood—

And concerning those matters which they seemed to have investigated with some certainty, they were nevertheless judged by their successors—who were taught otherwise by experience and more skillful observation—to have strayed far from the target of truth and the nature of things, as if they were looking at objects only through a **lattice** <term>lattice: original "transenna," a screen or window-grating that obscures a full view; used here metaphorically to mean seeing things only partially or unclearly</term>. 

If an **Art**—by the merciful gift of **GOD**, the author of all good—were to bring out into the open, revealed and visible, the inner secrets of nature that are wrapped in the thickest veils (and therefore hidden from most **Philosophers** <note>Philosophers: specifically natural philosophers, the precursors to modern scientists, who studied the physical world</note> who see less clearly), then not only would a great increase in perfection be added to the remaining arts—which are currently incomplete due to the hidden nature of things—but the knowledge of **GOD** would also be more refined. For if, as **Paul testifies** <note>original: "Paulo teste." This refers to the Apostle Paul's argument in the Epistle to the Romans (1:20) that the Creator's invisible attributes are clearly seen and understood through the things He has made in the physical world.</note>, **GOD** is granted to be known through the contemplation of natural things, then a consequent love and piety toward **GOD**, more ardent and fervent, would be stirred up in the hearts of the living.

*I will say nothing of the sweetest nourishment of the mind that arises from this art, nor of its uses and benefits poured out most abundantly upon the human race, for these are perceptible in themselves as being most delightful and most fruitful. But **Alchemy** <term>Alchemy: The art of chemical transformation and the investigation of the inner properties of matter</term> is an art of such a kind that it not only searches out and opens up both the **essences** and the **powers** of the most hidden things in nature, and brings them into the light and sight of men—removing those obscurities that have until now produced ignorance and folly in the **haters of chemistry** <note>original: "misochymicis," a polemical term used by alchemists to describe those who despise or reject the chemical arts</note>—but it also ennobles what is base. Furthermore, by bringing forth from hiding into the open air powers that are of the greatest value for **human health** <note>salutem: in this context, it refers to both physical healing and the general well-being of humanity</note>, it skillfully adorns them once again.*

*This art shines forth as the most eminent of all, second to none: because to no other is it given to unearth the inner secrets and the most deeply hidden parts of nature so elegantly, and to bring them forth so skillfully for human uses and various other purposes in many ways. If it is permitted to reason in agreement with **Paul** <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul’s argument in Romans 1:20, where he suggests that God's invisible attributes are understood through the things He has made.</note>, a more evident **knowledge of God** <note>original: "Dei notitia"</note> can be drawn from the practice of this art of **Alchemy** than even from the records of the **Sacred Scriptures** themselves. ### Dedication.

—and to those things which bring no less nourishment to the mind and common utility from their sciences and wisdom than others, it is most just that recognition should not be denied. These are the authors and cultivators of the divine art of Alchemy. Will you say they are few? I say, few are capable, and therefore they are few. But there are many more despisers, both the high and the low, the literate and the illiterate. Both of these groups are to be laughed at, and left to the judgment of the Magistrate <note>The term *Magistratus* here refers to civil authorities or high-ranking officials who oversee public order and justice</note> in turn. 

If the lowliest and most illiterate person pursues this divine art—and its practitioners—with sharp and undeserved hatred, then it will be the duty of the supreme and wiser Magistrate to justly punish that man. Such a person judges imprudently regarding an art he does not know, yet which is most useful to the Republic <note>original: *Reipublicae*—the state or common good</note>. The Magistrate should order him to focus instead on fulfilling his own duty, to which he was divinely appointed, and to bid farewell to higher matters for which he is unfit. This is the case unless, perhaps, he has been granted so much leisure, and possesses such surplus erudition and wisdom, that—led by some vain persuasion—he thinks it right to meddle in the business of others and rashly judge things he does not understand. But in such a case, it is the right of every practitioner to defend his art, and in the manner of Thamyris <note>A mythical Greek singer who was blinded and lost his voice after arrogantly challenging the Muses; used here to suggest that pretenders should be humbled when they challenge things beyond their reach</note> to receive such <term>smatterers</term> <note>original: *sciolos*—people with superficial knowledge who pretend to be experts</note>. I write nothing that should be rejected by any magistrate who looks out for the interests of all...

### Dedication.

*...worthy. One knows those smatterers <note>original: sciolos — people with superficial knowledge</note> to be meddlesome <note>original: πολυπράγμονας (polypragmonas) — busybodies or meddlers</note>, who rashly claim for themselves the power to observe and judge all professional fields indiscriminately. They are, so to speak, "all-consumers"* <note>original: πανεπρήμονας (panepremonas) — literally "all-burners," here used to describe critics who meddle in and ruin every subject they touch</note> *namely, those who rashly claim authority for themselves. But the insults and curses against this art by ill-occupied men of letters are by no means to be borne; they spew out their venom disguised with the fake colors of Philosophical doctrine. But if it is permitted for them to wickedly and most insultingly curse this most noble art—which is confirmed by the most learned records and the most substantial authority of so many ancient craftsmen and wise men—who, as a good and fair judge, will find fault with me? I have stood as a patron for this art, which has been provoked by most atrocious insults yet shines forth by its own nobility and truth, and of which I profess myself to be a most devoted student. I have done this to the best of my power and judgment* <note>original: κατὰ δύναμιν καὶ κρίσιν (kata dynamin kai krisin)</note>*, scattering the trifles of those idlers into smoke and defending the truth. Regarding the attack on this art—oh, the shame!—these most malicious calumniators, through their insulting, their sophistry, and their lying, have left nothing undone in the public eye. ### Dedication.

*...those who were making a show of being able to make the art hated by men of letters; I have undertaken to dissolve and undermine these attacks in this little work, so that the* <term>Chemical art</term> <note>original: arte Chymica — here referring to the broader discipline of chemistry and alchemy combined</note> *might be restored to its ancient brilliance and its genuine self. I leave the insults and slanders blathered against such a great art and its highest practitioners to be punished by* **GOD**—*against whom they are so ungratefully injurious, as He is the author of this art, as of all good things—and to the Magistrate. For it is entirely the duty of the Magistrate to love and cherish those arts profitable to the State, and consequently to support their industrious practitioners who skillfully exercise the art and provide for health more diligently than those slandering* <term>quacks</term> <note>original: medicastris — a derogatory term for incompetent or fraudulent physicians</note>; *it is the Magistrate's role to be a rampart against such absurd mockers. I have thought it right to dedicate this labor, such as it is, to* **YOUR EXCELLENCY** <note>original: I. V. E. — likely "Illustrissimae Vestrae Excellentiae"</note>, *because in a just defense of the divine art against so many giant-like mockers, it seemed to me I would need a patron of justice, and one not to be found just anywhere. For the art of Alchemy and chemical practitioners, as well as* <term>chemical-physicians</term> <note>original: Chymiatri — practitioners of iatrochemistry, who used mineral-based medicines rather than just herbs</note>, *are looked upon with such hostile eyes by everyone that there appears to be no place left to take refuge. But this is due not so much to ignorance, as to...*

### Dedication.

#### QUESTION I.
#### *Is Alchemy a part of Philosophy?*

<image-desc>Large woodcut ornamental initial N, intricately decorated with curling foliage and a small face appearing within the left side of the design.</image-desc>

NO philosopher will deny that physics <note>original: physica — in the 17th century, 'physics' referred to "natural philosophy," the study of nature and the physical universe as a whole.</note> is subordinate to philosophy, and for that reason, that their doctrine is a part of Philosophy. Since, therefore, chemistry <note>original: chymia</note> is also a subordinate science <term>subalternated</term> <note>original: subalternata — in Aristotelian logic, a 'subaltern' science is a specialized field (like optics or alchemy) that applies the general laws of a 'higher' science (like geometry or physics) to a specific subject.</note> to the teaching of physics, being occupied with the same subject matter, it must by right be considered a part of Philosophy. Aristotle, in context 75 of the first book of the *Posterior Analytics* <note>original: lib. 1. post — referring to Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics*, a foundational text on scientific logic and demonstration.</note>, grants the name of the "subalternating" science to the "subalternated" science. If, therefore, Physics is a part of Philosophy, alchemy will be as well. Likewise, if Physics exists as a part of Philosophy because it treats the subject of Philosophy, and since the subject of Alchemy is the same—differing only in the form or manner of its treatment—then <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the bottom of the page.</note>

...[these things] should by no means be proscribed from the field of philosophy. Minerals, metals, and vegetables are subjects of physics, *as treated in Aristotle’s fourth book of Meteorology and scattered elsewhere; these same things are also treated by alchemy, yet in another way and through a method diverse from that of the Physicist. Therefore, alchemy is a part of philosophy. For whatever art is occupied with a specific subject of philosophy, that will be a part of philosophy for it. But Alchemy concerns itself with the physical subjects of Philosophy, to be contemplated and worked upon in its own way. Therefore [it is a part].*

## QUESTION II.
->*Whether Alchemy is an art.*<-

A Vatinian hatred <note>original: Vatinianum odium — a proverbial expression meaning a deep-seated or undying hatred, named after a Roman official famously loathed by Cicero.</note> has extorted a denial from the haters of chemistry <term>misochymists</term> <note>from the Greek words for "hatred" and "alchemy."</note>, but their ignorance of the art is worthy of the lash. It has now been proved that chemistry is a part of Philosophy. Therefore, *it is also a science or an art.* For "art" <note>original: ἡ τέχνη (hē technē)</note> and "science" <note>original: ἐπιστήμη (epistēmē)</note> *do not differ in reality and essence, but only in* definition <note>original: λόγῳ (logō)</note>. *For the same* collection of principles <note>original: σύλληψις ἀξιωμάτων (syllepsis axiōmatōn)</note> *is called an art...*

<page-num>3</page-num>

...[it is an art] when it is applied to production, through which some work must be accomplished. It is called a **Science** by reason of the principles of its operation, which are constructed from causes and other scientific grounds. **Art** is defined by Aristotle <note>referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book VI</note> as *a productive habit involving true reason.* According to Lucian's definition <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century rhetorician</note>, art is *a system of well-conceived perceptions practiced together toward some useful end in life* <note>original Greek: σύστημα τῶν ἐυκαταλήψεων ἐγγεγυμνασμένων, πρός τι τὸ τέλος ἐύχρηστον τῶν ἐν βίῳ.</note>. Therefore, to whatever thing the definition applies, the term being defined also applies. The definition of an "art" applies to Chemistry. Therefore, it is an art. For it consists of uniform precepts arranged in a methodical form and order.

Its duty is to draw out the purest essences <term>juices</term> <note>original: succos — often refers to the essential liquids or "soups" extracted from raw materials.</note> from heterogeneous <note>diverse or mixed</note> things, or to make them more excellent in the nobility and purity of their substance, and in their powers and effects. This they call **exalting**, or **grading**, and sometimes **subliming** <note>Sublimation involves heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, a process used to purify substances.</note>. This is achieved both according to the essence and the combined qualities and powers of the materials—now by adding something, now by subtracting, now by altering, sometimes by **transmuting** and begetting one thing from the destruction <note>original: corrupto — in the Aristotelian sense where the "corruption" of one form allows for the "generation" of another.</note> of another, sometimes by joining, and through whatever other crafts there may be. Every art consists in production, according to Aristotle’s definition, and must be undertaken with **right reason** <note>original: *recta ratio* — a central concept in Aristotelian ethics referring to the practical wisdom required to act correctly.</note>. All mechanical arts strive toward this end, so that they may diligently pursue the purpose of their crafts; for instance, the art of shoemaking cannot fashion a shoe without the separation of the bad from the good. The "bad" in that craft is the heterogeneous material, which is unsuitable for constructing the work and is therefore to be cast out. The chemical art acts in a similar fashion. *It is therefore an art, and not a figment.*

For a figment has no established precepts, no skillfully crafted work existing in nature, and no use in itself. Yet all these qualities, and even more significant ones belonging to true art, are present in the chemical art. Therefore, it is not merely the product of a fictional or delusional imagination. To suggest that separating form from matter is the same as separating good from evil is a delusion; both are good, because **to be** is better than **not to be** <note>original Greek: τὸ εἶναι (*to einai*) better than τῷ μὴ εἶναι (*to mē einai*); a classical philosophical axiom asserting that existence is inherently preferable to non-existence.</note>.

### QUESTION 4.

->*Whether Salt, Mercury, and Sulphur are the constitutive principles of perfectly mixed bodies.*<-
<note>The "constitutive principles" (*principia συστατικά*) are the primary components that make up a substance. In the chemical philosophy of this period, these three—Salt, Mercury, and Sulphur—were known as the "Tria Prima."</note>

Those who claim that these principles are manufactured <note>original: *factitia*</note> argue that they have received a different form from the artificial fire than their native one; thus, they are not implanted by nature, but acquired through art. But this argument ignores the **logical refutation** <term>elenchus</term> <note>A term from Aristotelian logic referring to a cross-examination that proves a contradiction in the opponent's thesis.</note>. For although these principles come into view through the work of artificial fire, no one will deny that art here strives for nothing other than **to tear apart what has been put together, and to dissolve what has been composed** <note>original Greek: τὸ διασπᾶν τὰ συγκείμενα, καὶ τὸ συντιθέμενα διαλύειν (*to diaspan ta synkeimena, kai to syntithemena dialyein*)</note>. 

Separation creates no new forms or things, nor is the arrangement or disposition of any art sufficient in itself, unless a material is provided to be managed by that art. It is therefore ridiculous to say that the principles are artificial and manufactured simply because the craftsman, using the instrument of artificial fire, has finally brought them forth. Why are they not likewise considered natural principles, since they are released by a natural organ—which is fire? For fire in the hand of the craftsman is as much natural as it is artificial:

<page-num>8</page-num>
<header>Exercises</header>

...it is not the role of fire to fabricate forms, nor is it the nature of fire to always procreate the same things from diverse materials. Yet, from all mixed bodies, fire produces <term>Salt, Mercury, and Sulfur</term> <note>Known as the *tria prima*, these were the three fundamental components of matter in early modern "spagyric" or Paracelsian chemistry.</note>. Therefore, these things do not come into existence by the power of fire alone. Furthermore, fire is simple and uniform in its action, even when a craftsman attempts a separation; therefore, fire cannot be the author of contrary substances through one and the same action. 

And how could it be the author, when the craftsman—and fire, which is the craftsman’s tool—are entirely devoid and empty of the power of these three principles? As Aristotle says in *Physics*, Book 2, text 21: **"Whatever is produced by art possesses no innate impulse for change"** <note>original Greek: ὅσον δὲ ἔστιν ἀπὸ τέχνης οὐδεμίαν ὁρμὴν ἔχει μεταβολῆς ἔμφυτον (*hoson de estin apo technēs oudemian hormēn echei metabolēs emphyton*).</note>.

Therefore, by clear argument, the principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury are natural things derived from Nature. A specific effect argues for a specific cause. In this process, a separation of **heterogeneous principles** <note>Substances that are different in kind or nature from one another.</note> occurs. It follows that this separation argues for its own cause, which is heat. The proper function of heat is **to separate** <note>original Greek: διακρίνειν (*diakrinein*)</note>, whereas the function of cold is **to bring together** <note>original Greek: συνισάνε (*synistane*); likely a variation of *synistanai*, meaning to solidify or compose.</note>. 

"Heat is," says Aristotle, **"that which brings together things of the same kind; for the 'separating' that they say fire does is actually a 'bringing together' of things of the same nature. For it results in the removal of foreign substances"** <note>original Greek: θερμὸν ἔστιν... τὸ συγκρῖνον τὰ ὁμογενῆ τὸ γὰρ διακρίνειν ὥσπερ φάσι ποιεῖν τὸ πῦρ συγκρίνειν ἐστὶ, τὰ ὁμόφυλα. <header>Alchemy, Question 4.</header>

...those who speak in opposition. That from which a thing is made, being innate and remaining within it, is the **matter** of that thing.

And yet, celestial heat generates all things from the four **Elements** <note>The classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>. Therefore, they argue, these elements are the <term>proximate matter</term> <note>The immediate material from which something is formed; for example, flour is the proximate matter of bread, while grain is its remote matter.</note> of <term>sublunary things</term> <note>Refers to the Earthly realm "below the moon," which was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the perfect heavens.</note>, and not Sulfur, Salt, and Mercury. This conclusion is denied.

For even if the initial proposition is granted, it does not follow that the elements are the **proximate** matter of sublunary things; rather, from the preceding premise, it only follows that the elements are the [remote] matter of sublunary things. However, repeat the proposition and consider this: all things are forged from the three principles of **Salt, Mercury, and Sulfur**. Therefore, it is utterly absurd to claim that the four elements are the proximate matter of sublunary things. Proximate matter is endowed with "proximate potentiality," so that when the active causes are present and nothing stands in the way, it is necessary for that thing to become what it was potentially within the matter. 

From where, then, do so many dissimilar, <term>heterogeneous</term> <note>Substances made of diverse or unlike parts.</note> compounds come? To what purpose are so many kinds of **seeds**? This would be the result if all sublunary things consisted immediately of the elements. Is human reason also derived immediately from the elements?

...[the Che]mists, relying on these same repeated arguments, will demonstrate far more firmly that bodies consist of three principles: **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury**. The elements do not combine in such a way that they are completely destroyed, but rather so that they are no longer "actually" <note>original: "actu." In medieval philosophy, "actual" refers to what a thing is right now, as opposed to its "potential."</note> what they were previously when separate; yet they retain their potential power <note>original: "potentiam"</note> within the mass of the body. For the Chemists, besides these three Aristotelian foundations, an abundance of sensory evidence also provides support. 

In the dissolution <note>The chemical process of breaking down a substance into its constituent parts, often through heat or acid.</note> of a mineral or metal, you will recognize the power of **Sulfur** through the nose <note>Sulfur was associated with strong odors, particularly when burned.</note> and through reason. With your eyes, you may judge the same from the resulting flame. In plants and animals, even if you deny the power <note>original: δύναμιν (dynamin)</note> of evident sensory proof, you must nevertheless prove the presence of the principles of **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury**, granted that they exist potentially and not "actually" within the mixed elements. Thus, even if you cannot point to literal sulfur itself during the breaking down of a mixture, you can nonetheless identify a "sulfurous" quality, and likewise a "mercurial" or "salty" quality.

In minerals and metals, it is clear that they exist in "actuality" <note>original: "actu." For both come from nature, because they are the constituents <note>original: συστατικοὶ (*systatikoi*), meaning the components that form the very structure of a substance.</note> of natural things; and even if they are not the ultimate principles themselves, they are nonetheless composed from them. It is not by art, therefore, for it is not the role of art to manufacture everything while nature is denied.

# QUESTION VI

## *Whether all things resolve into the three chemical principles: Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt.*

If these chemical principles are understood **analogically** <note>original: *Analogice*. This means interpreting the terms not as literal substances, but as symbols for qualities: Mercury for fluidity/spirit, Sulfur for combustibility, and Salt for solidity/fixity.</note>, we can agree with them, so that <gloss>for</gloss> <note>The original shorthand "p̃" stands for the Latin *pro* (for).</note> Mercury, **water** is substituted; for Sulfur, **fire** and **air**; and for Salt, **earth**. **If the analogy is denied**, then the claim that all things resolve into them is also denied. 

Consider a sticky mud made from water and earth; see how it is bound together and hardened into a stone, just as we observe happening in nature. If this stone were to be broken down into its final components, it would be resolved not into Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt, but into the **common and physical principles** <note>original: *vulgata & physica... principia*. This refers to the four classical Aristotelian elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, which were the "common" explanation in the universities of the time.</note>. 

What of the elements themselves? Do they ever fall back into those [chemical] principles, seeing as they were never composed of them in the first place? And what of minerals? Not all of them, even when repeatedly exhausted by the fire, yield these three principles; instead, they yield now this, now that, especially to the 
->art.<- <note>original: *arti*. In this context, "Art" refers to the practice of Alchemy or Chemistry.</note>

## QUESTION VII.

->*Is the Physician and the Chemist the same?*<-
->*It is denied.*<-

The different subjects that occupy each of them distinguish the two; therefore, it is necessary for the chemist and the physician to be distinct from one another. The Physician is one who knows medicine and employs it well for the procurement of health. Or, one who <term>treats well</term> <note>original Greek: *eu therapeuei* (εὖ θεραπεύει). This emphasizes the clinical application of medical knowledge to a patient's recovery.</note>. The Chemist does not have "health" as his primary subject of study; rather, through his own zeal, he explores the very natures of things by the unique art of **resolutions**, **separations**, or **exaltations** <note>These are the three core stages of alchemical labor: *Resolution* (breaking a substance down), *Separation* (isolating the pure from the impure), and *Exaltation* (raising a substance to a more potent or refined state).</note>. From these processes, he provides excellent medicines to the physician in a secondary role and supplies the suitable material for healing.

# Alchemy, Question 11.

Through separation <note>original Greek: *διακρίσει* (*diakrisei*), meaning the act of distinguishing or separating components.</note>, there will come into your sight something oily, something watery, and something dry; any one of these will still be a mixture and not a simple substance, because the original mixture was not made from pure, simple elements. # On Alchemy, Question II.

...is given and nourished <note>Continuing the sentence from the previous page: "is proven by the [fact that] a decoction or distilled water..."</note> by the decoction or distilled water being prescribed. You do not wish for the entire composition <term>Composition: Often referred to by the Greek-derived term *crasis*, meaning the specific blend or "mixture" of qualities that defines a substance.</term> of all the mixed parts to be exhibited, but only a certain power of these things, determined by its own composition—unless you persuade yourself that distilled water possesses the entire temperament <note>In early medicine, "temperament" was the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> of the mixtures. 

But the residue teaches us that the whole temperament of the mixtures is not present in those distilled waters, as the residue still yields much of its strength through more refined digestion <term>Digestion: In alchemy, a process where a substance is subjected to gentle, continuous heat to break it down or "ripen" it.</term> and distillation. A decoction of Rhubarb <note>Latin: *Rhenbarbari*.</note> possesses the virtue of purging bile <note>original Greek: *cholagogein*</note> and drawing it out, while the astringent quality—which pertains to the temperament of the whole—remains behind in the residue and the more earthy part, which is the proper subject for astringency. 

Therefore, let the composition of the whole be absent from the separation of the three principles <term>The Three Principles: In the alchemical system of Paracelsus, these are Salt (body/solidity), Sulphur (soul/oiliness), and Mercury (spirit/liquidity).</term> if they are not joined together again; nevertheless, let the result be furnished with its own specific and determined composition, and let this be for a good use. ### QUESTION XII.
->*Whether Salt, as one of the natural principles, should be considered artificial since it is produced by art?*<-

Those who despise chemistry <note>Latin: misochymici, literally "chemistry-haters."</note> argue that whatever is a fundamental principle of nature cannot be an artificial product. They claim that the Salt produced by chemists is an artificial creation. Therefore, they conclude, it cannot be a natural principle. This conclusion must be denied, and the premise must be answered as follows: the Salt of the chemists is called "artificial" only because the art of chemistry purifies its nature and restores it to its proper integrity; meanwhile, in and of itself, it retains the <term>Logos: The essential reason, definition, or inner logic that makes a thing what it is.</term> <note>original Greek: λόγον</note> of a principle.

## QUESTION XV.

->*Whether salts, revered by medical antiquity, were prepared, understood, and used through the process of calcination.*<-

Truly, we read in Aegina <note>original: *Æginetam*; referring to Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician whose medical encyclopedia was a standard reference for centuries.</note> in his *Book on Remedies*, Book 7, Chapter 11, that for the preparation of "theriacal salts" <note>original: *salium theriacalium*; salts derived from theriac, a legendary ancient compound used as a universal antidote and general medicine.</note>, he selected vipers—those most venomous of reptiles—which were seasoned and thoroughly wrapped in **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a naturally occurring mineral salt used in both metal-working and medicine.</term>, **gentian**, **birthwort** <note>original: *aristolochia*; a plant used in ancient medicine, often associated with childbirth and treating snakebites.</note>, **centaury**, **cardamom**, and various other simple medicines of that kind. 

Then, once all these ingredients had been combined and bound into a paste using **Attic honey** <note>Honey from the mountains near Athens, highly prized in the ancient world for its purity and medicinal properties.</note>, he orders them to be placed in an earthen pot reinforced with "very strong clay" <term>luto fortissimo: likely "lute," a specialized clay or cement used to seal alchemical vessels and protect them from high heat.</term>. This pot is covered with its own lid, which must however be pierced with holes so that whatever poisonous vapor remains may evaporate. He then directs it to be exposed to a **reverberatory fire** <term>reverberatory fire: an alchemical furnace design where the heat is reflected or "reverberated" from the roof of the furnace onto the material, allowing for extremely high temperatures without the fuel touching the medicine.</term>, so that the contents may be entirely reduced to **lime and ashes**. 

From these remains, with the addition and mixing of other substances, the theriacal salts are made and prepared. This entire operation is purely chemical, and it clearly proves that the ancients—

Because of this, the bodily form is in one case reversible or reducible, while in the other it is not.

Furthermore, **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air or oxygen to change its physical or chemical state, often to produce a powder</term>, simply so called, occurs sometimes by waters, sometimes by fires. By waters, it occurs through **corrosion** or dilution. **Corrosion** uses mineral waters mixed with vegetable ones. That which is carried out by fire or dry heat is completed either by burning—and this either by **sublimating** <term>sublimating: the process where a solid turns directly into a gas without passing through a liquid state</term> or **precipitating**—so that they become either ashes of vegetables or the **calxes** <note>original: *calces*; the crumbly residue left after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly burned</note> of minerals. This happens either immediately or through the later intervention of other things, such as air, water, a hammer, a mill, and so on.

Or, it is completed without combustion through the dispersion of a molten substance; or by hardening through vapor or by the addition of something brittle. If, by any of these methods of calcining, either the **constitution** <term>constitution: the specific balance of qualities (*crasis*) that defines a substance</term> or the moisture is lost...

-># Preliminary Exercises<-

[...the primordial moisture] <note>This completes the thought from the previous page regarding the preservation of essential fluids.</note> will be preserved whole and restored by the remaining methods of the art. Indeed, the artisan will deny that the **constitution** <term>constitution: original Latin: *crasis* (from Greek *krasis*); the specific "mixture" or "blend" of qualities that defines a substance's unique nature</term> of the thing being calcined perishes in any way, or that the **primordial moisture** <term>primordial moisture: original: *humidum primogenium*; in alchemical theory, this was the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid that resided deep within matter</term> is dissipated.

If one or the other goes to ruin, it happens by accident, occurring through the ignorance of a destroyer rather than the skill of an artisan. The greatest difficulty, especially in calcination by violent fire, is to keep the **temperament** <note>original: *temperiem*; the balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within a substance</note> of the thing whole. This is a feat belonging only to an artisan skilled through long experience. It is very difficult to achieve in vegetables <note>meaning plants and organic matter</note>, but easier in minerals and metals.

If the **salt** <note>In this context, the "salt" refers to the solid, purified remains of a substance after it has been burned or processed.</note> still carries the scent of the substance’s own specific powers, would you say its constitution is destroyed, or its primordial moisture taken away? On the contrary, every salt prepared by an artisan represents the nature of the calcined thing as closely as possible, as confirmed by the effects of its medical use. 

Therefore, the substance will retain its primordial moisture and its constitution during the process of calcination. This is also supported by the argument that a native **oily substance** <note>original: *oleosa substantia*; alchemists believed the "sulfur" or oil of a plant contained its soul or active essence</note> can be extracted by art from many salts; therefore, it must have remained [to be...]

If you truly cure all your patients with sweets, why then do you provide acidic and cooling remedies, or trouble the sick with such unpleasant, very bitter substances?

Quicksilver <note>original: *Argentum vivum*</note> unites with arsenic and sulfur because of the affinity <note>original: *symbolum*; a term used to describe a "likeness" or shared qualities between different substances.</note> and familiarity it has with them. In cinnabar, copper, and lead, quicksilver solidifies naturally, though it can be separated from them again as a volatile substance through the artist's skill. And what else is lead, other than quicksilver in its first stage of fixation within the metallic family? Therefore, it also mixes with lead quite easily. Do you want more arguments for quicksilver being the principle of metals?

Why, then, are these remedies slanderously accused of being poison? Why are mineral and metallic baths not removed from the list of poisons? That remedy, for which all other medicines are tried in vain...

## QUESTION XXIII.

->Should chemical remedies be rejected or accused of being some kind of poison because they lack a similarity to the human body?<-

->By no means.<-

If this were true, then no remedies at all should be accepted, because no remedies possess a similarity—neither in their physical substance nor in their qualities—to the body they are meant to treat. Furthermore, there is no need for such a similarity in either common <note>original: *vulgariū*, referring to traditional Galenic herbal medicines available at any apothecary</note> or chemical remedies. In fact, for a substance to have the power to alter the body, it is so far from needing any similarity that, if such a likeness were required, the substance would no longer fit the definition of a medicine's power to act. A medicine must be **antipathetic** <term>acting through opposition; the principle that a disease is cured by its opposite, such as treating a "hot" fever with a "cold" herb</term> so that it can drive out corrupt **humors** <term>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—whose balance was thought to determine health</term> by means of that very opposition. 

However, if they wish to attribute to chemical remedies that same kind of "similarity" which they claim for traditional medicines according to the mind of **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–210 AD), the ancient physician whose theories formed the basis of Western medicine for 1,500 years</note>, then chemical remedies will also act through that similarity, even when they have been prepared by the **spagyric art** <term>another name for alchemy, specifically the process of separating, purifying, and recombining the "essences" of natural substances</term>.

# Alchemy, Question 25.

...from the Delphic tripod, clearly. But let the asses remain among the Cumans <note>A Latin proverb (Asinus apud Cumanos) referring to a fool who tries to pass himself off as someone important or wise, based on an Aesop's fable about a donkey in a lion's skin.</note>.

However, it is rightly asked: *how does it happen that strong medicines are considered destructive and poisonous by some, while "benign" medicines are thought to lack poisonous qualities?* If they are to be judged by the harm they inflict on the human body, why are the "benign" ones excused when they are equally harmful to the body? If you say that harm occurs from the former incidentally <term>original: *κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς*; a philosophical term meaning a secondary or accidental effect rather than an essential quality</term>, I would argue in turn that the same happens with the latter.

In their own right, all medicines accepted thus far have been useful to the human body by drawing out harmful juices <note>original: *succos*; referring to the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> from it, <term>expelling phlegm, expelling bile, and expelling black bile</term>. The only difference is this: the mild medicines perform their actions with a lighter force, while the strong ones act with a more powerful and "carrying" force, as it were. 

Thus, <term>the process of purging</term> is common to all of them when considered in themselves; they do not differ in their fundamental nature, even if certain ones are specifically designated to stir up particular humors. For by the same virtue that Rhubarb rouses a harmful humor, so too does scammony <note>original: *diagrydium*; a potent resin extracted from the root of the scammony plant, used as a drastic purgative.</note>; both possess a bile-purging <term>original: *cholagogum*; a substance that promotes the discharge of bile from the system</term> character.

### Alchemia, Question 25.

...originating from the Delphic tripod, <note>original: *pode Delphico*; referring to the tripod upon which the Pythia sat to deliver oracles, here used sarcastically to describe the "divine" but empty pronouncements of traditionalists</note> clearly. It is rightly asked: *how does it happen that strong medicines, which are considered deleterious and poisonous by others, are indeed poisonous, while the benign ones are considered to be lacking in poisonous quality?* If they are to be judged as such because of the harm they inflict upon the human body, why are the "benign" ones excused when they are equally harmful to the body? If you should say that the harm occurs here <term>incidentally</term> <note>original: *κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς* (kata symbebēkos); a philosophical term meaning a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing</note>, I will infer in turn that the same thing happens in the other case through regular use.

To this point, all medicines accepted for use have been beneficial to the human body by drawing out harmful <term>humors</term> <note>original: *succos*; literally "juices." In Galenic medicine, these are the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that must stay in balance for health.</note> from it, <term>expelling the phlegm, expelling the yellow bile, and expelling the black bile</term> <note>original: *καὶ τὸ φλέγμα φυγγάνειν καὶ τὸ χολαφυγγάνειν καὶ μελανφυγγάνειν* (kai to phlegma phygganein kai to cholaphygganein kai melanphygganein)</note>. There is only this distinction: that the latter perform their actions with a lighter force, while the former do so with a stronger and, as it were, more driving force. Thus, <term>to be purged</term> <note>original: *τὸ καθαίρεσθαι* (to kathairesthai)</note> is common to all these substances when considered in themselves; they do not differ in their entire nature, even if some are specifically defined to stir up particular humors. For by whatever power Rhubarb rouses a harmful humor, by that same power <term>diagrydium</term> <note>A medicinal preparation made from the juice of the scammony plant, often mixed with quince juice to moderate its harshness.</note> does so as well; both are considered <term>cholagogues</term> <note>original: *cholagogū*; a substance that promotes the discharge of bile from the system.</note>.

# Alchemy, Question 26.

The first point, being a bare assertion, could simply be denied in passing. However, so that we do not simply affirm or deny things while others speak without any reason, we deny that the temperament of the purging substance can be removed. 

A person intending to distill a cathartic medicine skillfully either tries to drive it through an **alembic** <term>alembic</term> <note>an ancient distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube; the "head" catches the vapor</note> or to let it settle to the bottom. Therefore, wherever the substance is moved, the quality follows its own proper subject as a companion. For the elements possess a far more excellent power of altering than the "elementated" <note>original: *elementatis*; physical substances or medicines composed of the elements, rather than the pure elements themselves.</note> things themselves. ## QUESTION XXX.

### *Whether, if the substantial form is destroyed, the mixture remains intact as the primary cause of medical powers?*

Those who dare to assert this believe that the <term>crāsis</term> <note>original: *crasin*; a term from ancient medicine and alchemy referring to the specific "mixture" or "temperament" of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that defines a body's character.</note> of a natural thing takes the place of the <term>substantial form</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "substantial form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is; for example, the soul is the substantial form of a living body.</note> that constitutes the compound. They ascribe all specific <term>properties</term> <note>original Greek: *ἰδιότητας* (*idiotētas*); the unique characteristics or "peculiarities" of a substance that give it specific powers, such as a herb's ability to heal.</note> to this mixture, arguing that these properties remain even when the substantial form has been cast out. 

But in truth, since every mixture is either a quality or something composed of qualities—and since such a thing is merely an <term>accident</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential characteristic. For example, being "tall" or "hot" is an accident, while being a "human" or "gold" is the substance. The author argues that a mixture of qualities cannot be the "essence" of a thing.</note>—it is impossible for an accident to constitute a substance. It is strange that the nature of primary "principles" is so recklessly attributed to a mere accidental mixture, especially since it is asserted in Aristotle's *Metaphysics* that a principle is, by its very nature, ungenerable <note>In this context, "ungenerable" means it cannot be created by combining other, more basic things; it is a fundamental building block.</note>. Furthermore, in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, he demonstrates that the form itself—which constitutes the essence of a thing—is neither an element nor a com- <note>The word is likely "composite" (*compositum*), continuing on the next page. This refers to the idea that the "form" of a thing is a single, simple reality, not a collection of parts.</note>

Nor can the mixture exist without the form, nor the form without the mixture; and yet, these two differ entirely in their essence.

Indeed, the mixture can be called the "form of the compound," but it is not the <term>substantial form</term> <note>The "substantial form" is the essential "blueprint" that makes an object a specific kind of thing (e.g., what makes a rose a rose).</note>. This is because the mixture arises from qualities—and when those qualities are altered, the mixture is created—but it is not "substantial," for it is not the nature of qualities to constitute a <term>specific individual thing</term> <note>original Greek: *τὸ δέ τι* (*to de ti*); a technical term in Aristotelian philosophy referring to a distinct, individual substance.</note>. 

Furthermore, it is clear by this argument that the mixture is not the form itself, nor the nature of the thing, since the mixture is said to *be present according to nature*. Those things that are "present according to nature" are not the nature itself. For, according to Aristotle, there is a difference between Nature, a natural thing, and that which is said to be present "according to nature." Therefore, although the substantial form of natural and living things may perish while the properties and the mixture remain unharmed and survive, it follows nevertheless—

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into the nature of matter and form, building on the previous page's distinction between a physical mixture (crasis) and the "substantial form" that gives a thing its essential identity.</meta>

<page-num>97</page-num>
<header>Alchemy, Question 30.</header>

It is not the case that these inanimate things consist solely of a <term>mixture</term> <note>original: *crasi*; the physical temperament or blend of qualities like heat and moisture.</note> and accidental properties. To claim that such things could exist on their own and serve as the foundation for others is utterly absurd. Instead, even when the "vegetative" power is abolished, a <term>natural form</term> <note>The essential blueprint that remains in a substance even after it loses the capacity for life or growth.</note> can remain, establishing the essence of the compound. Aristotle, in the ninth book of his *Metaphysics*, distinguishes between the matters and forms of natural things. For there is a certain <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: *materia prima*; the most basic, formless substrate that has the potential to become any physical thing.</note>, which possesses the potential to be subjected to all forms. 

There is another kind, the "ultimate" or "native" matter, which he calls the <term>final and proper matter</term> <note>original Greek: *ἐσχάτω καὶ οἰκείαν ὕλην* (*eschatōn kai oikeian hylēn*).</note>. This matter is subjected to only one <term>substantial form</term> <note>The core identity that makes a thing what it is.</note>; it exists simultaneously with this form and perishes along with it. Furthermore, there is another type of matter that precedes the final form in the process of <term>generation</term> <note>The natural process of coming-into-being or creation.</note>. This matter cannot exist at the same time as the ultimate matter; instead, when the ultimate matter is shaped by a form, the previous state is destroyed, and the prior form within that matter is abolished and dies away. 

For example, if blood is being made, the form of <term>chyle</term> <note>A milky fluid produced during digestion that was thought to be the precursor to blood.</note> ceases to be. And when flesh is made from blood, the "species" (or specific nature) of blood ceases to exist within the matter that succeeds it as flesh. There are, however, certain forms that come earlier in <term>generation</term> <note>original Greek: *γενέσει* (*genesei*); the process of birth or formation.</note> within living bodies, which [lead] to the later ones...

## QUESTION XXXI.

->*Should antidotes be classified among poisons?*<-

->It is denied.<-

*If <term>antidotes</term> <note>original: *alexipharmaca*; derived from the Greek words for "to ward off" and "poison."</note> are contained under the category of poisons, then antidotes would not be remedies for poisons. But they are indeed remedies for poisons. For that is precisely why they are called alexipharmaca. Therefore [they are not poisons]. ...yet they might seem to be placed in the same category, both poisons and <term>antidotes</term> <note>original: *alexipharmaca*; specifically medicines used to neutralize or ward off poison.</note>, because opposites are of the same kind, even though these opposites themselves are by no means to be equated with one another. It may be that many poisonous ingredients were added through the error of authors or those mixing the antidotes or protective remedies.

Why does the <term>malfunctioning bile</term> <note>original: *bilis peccans*; a Galenic term for a "sinning" or morbid humor that has become corrupted or excessive, causing disease.</note> not provide as much aid to itself as **Rhubarb** provides to malfunctioning bile in cases of **jaundice**, liver obstruction, and so on—especially when the bile is the dominant force in terms of quantity? What is this "action" of Rhubarb by which it draws out bile that is supposedly similar to it? It must be an action of the whole substance; therefore, it cannot be an action of the qualities alone, for no natural action belongs to qualities by themselves, as they are merely <term>accidents</term> <note>original: *accidentia*; in Aristotelian philosophy, these are properties like color, heat, or dryness that cannot exist independently of a physical body.</note>. Nor could this action of Rhubarb arise from the qualities of bile—suppose, for instance, heat and dryness. For if that were the case, everything endowed with those two qualities would stir up bile, which is a baseless claim. 

The action, therefore, belongs to the whole substance and is specific to it. If, then, it is deprived of its own proper action (by which it is supposedly linked to bile by similarity), how can it be transformed into the substance of the humor it is meant to move if this very action is hindered? Or is it by the benefit of something else? Surely not the qualities? For no transformation occurs through them.

The first premise is true, as every skillfully made distillate proves most clearly. Therefore, the second premise is also true. 

To prove the first point by the example of common market-women <note>original: *anicularum denicarum*; literally "common little old women," here referring to local herb-sellers or housewives who made simple remedies.</note>, which is not to be dismissed (for the operations of master craftsmen are perhaps too noble to fit within your understanding): Taste their cinnamon water. ## QUESTION XXXVI.
### *Is the juice the soul of the plant?*

Whoever judges so foolishly is gripped by a **frenzy** <note>original: *paraphrenitide*; a medical term for delirium or mental inflammation.</note>. That juice, insofar as it is juice, exists in all living things; how then can it be the soul of a plant? Is the plant's juice its **vegetative soul** <note>The most basic level of the soul in Aristotelian philosophy, responsible for nutrition and growth.</note>? Or is it the plant’s **natural form** <note>The essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is.</note>? It is not the former, because once the plant is cut and deprived of it, it ceases to grow. Is it the latter then? But a natural form not only gives shape to the whole, it also defines its boundaries. It is not within the nature of juice by itself to give form or life, as it lacks all form of its own; much less can it define boundaries, as it relies on—and must be held in by—the boundaries of another substance. Is it a natural thing—a **specific individual substance** <note>original: *to de ti* (τὸ δέ τι); a Greek Aristotelian term for a concrete, individual "this" thing.</note>—which has been deprived of its own soul? Most plants are juiceless, [without] juice...

## QUESTION XL.

### *Whether Masteries, tinctures, salts, and oils are*
### *portions of matter?*

A **Mastery** <term>Magisterium: in early chemistry, a preparation where a substance is purified and "ennobled" while retaining its full medicinal identity, often considered a "masterwork" of the chemist</term> is the essence of the whole, but purified and ennobled by chemical works: therefore, it is not a portion of matter alone. That which possesses the whole must also necessarily have the integrating part. But the reverse is not true. How then is a Mastery a portion of matter? One tincture is simple, another compound; each participates in the **crasis** <term>crasis: the specific temperament or "blending" of qualities that defines a substance's nature</term> of the substance providing the tint, though one more so than the other. ...[substan]ce of the mixture, influenced by its own color, a **tincture**. 
**Essence** belongs not to the matter alone, much less to a tiny portion of it, but to the whole. The same reasoning applies to **oils**, which contain little to nothing of the physical matter, being influenced in their **form** <note>the defining essence or organizing principle of a thing</note> more than their material. Nor can **salts** be the offspring of matter alone, even if they are taken from the *caput mortuum* <term>caput mortuum: literally "dead head," the dregs or useless residue left behind after a chemical substance has been distilled or burned</term>; for they are pregnant with spirits, both fixed and volatile, which are specific qualities joined not to the matter, but to the whole and especially to the **form**. 

It is ridiculous to claim that matter is an evil, and that **spagyric** <term>spagyric: a term for alchemical medicine, from the Greek words for "separating" and "combining"</term> remedies—being born from matter and "evil"—are gripped by that same malice; as the saying goes, "from a bad crow comes a bad egg" <note>original Greek: κακοῦ κώρακος κακὸν ᾠον (kakou korakos kakon oon)</note>. If **primary matter** <note>the pure, undifferentiated substrate of all physical things</note> is evil in itself, the Philosopher <note>a common title for Aristotle</note> does not consider it so, except by the name of **privation** <note>original Greek: στερήσεως (stereseos); the philosophical idea that "evil" is not a physical thing, but merely the absence or "privation" of a proper form or good</note> attached to it. If things arising from it were evil simply because matter itself was "evil," then I ask: what would *not* be evil? For all things proceed from matter, which serves as their common subject and underlying foundation.

## QUESTION XLIV.

->Whether mineral remedies and others made by chemical<-
->apparatus become hotter than they were in themselves<-
->and more corrosive by fire,<-
->or not?<-

The "haters of chemistry" <note>original Latin: *Misochymici*; a term used to describe physicians who opposed the new chemical medicines of the Renaissance</note> falsely claim that chemical remedies are not only made worse by fire, but even become deadly. Do they really become hotter, or even deadly? From where, I ask you, would they contract such a deadly power? From the fire? But fire is not deadly in itself; it is a simple element. Perhaps they contained something deadly within them beforehand? By what argument could you prove that? By none. Even if a substance contained some poison, do you not believe all of that would vanish in the heat of the fire? We see that the innate heat of hens and other animals that feed on poisonous things "tames" <note>original: *edomantur*; literally "subdued" or "broken in" like a wild animal</note> those poisons; why should the same not be true of active <term>drastikō <gloss>effective or powerful</gloss></term> fire? Even snakes, once boiled, can be eaten without harm, as the poison is cast off through the steam and the cooking broth. Despite this, our opponents further strive to prove that substances become hotter and more corrosive through fire by using both logic and the authority of two great figures: one being Aristotle and the other Galen. Their logic is this: the heat of metals...

...which is inherent in all things, is intensified by the addition of external heat. Therefore, chemical remedies that are hot by nature become even hotter by fire. But the hater of chemistry <note>original: *misochymicus*; a term for those who rejected the chemical medicines of Paracelsus in favor of traditional herbalism</note> ignores the logical rebuttal <note>original: *elenchum*; a formal logical refutation</note>. Suppose metals are hot, and a more vehement fire is applied: will the internal heat of the metals not be dissipated by the stronger fire, rather than being intensified? If fire draws out the internal heat of other things, it will surely do the same to metals, acting as it always does according to its own nature. But the former point is more true than the latter. Therefore, fire will not spare the heat of the metals.

The authorities of Galen and Aristotle are also brought forward. Specifically, Galen in Book 2 of *On the Composition of Medicaments According to Kinds* <note>original Greek: *κατὰ γένη* (kata gene)</note> claims that metals are rendered biting <note>original: *mordacia*; referring to substances that sting, corrode, or irritate the skin</note> through contact with fire. Likewise, Aristotle in Book 2 of *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 2, and Galen in Book 2 of *On the Natural Faculties*, teach that all burnt things become hotter than they were originally, using the example of a torch that has been burnt versus one that has not.

I respond: Galen, if read with faithful eyes, is so far from claiming that such remedies become sharper and more eroding by fire; rather, he asserts that those things which are sharp are rendered less hot and less biting by burning, and that they lay aside all their corrosive quality if they are washed in water.

### QUESTION 48.
->*Is Hydrargyros, or quicksilver, a poison?*<-
->It is denied.<-

Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a renowned Italian physician and botanist</note> reports that *quicksilver is given with difficulty to women in labor in the weight of a scruple* <term>scruple: an apothecaries' weight equal to about 1.3 grams</term>. Others administer two millet-grains’ worth of it for intestinal worms, and both Falloppio <note>Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562), a major figure in the history of anatomy</note> has written and veterinarians know that this is done most safely in beasts of burden. 

Alessandro Massaria <note>1523–1598, an Italian medical professor</note>, in *Book 2 of On the Plague, page 54*, denies along with Falloppio that **mercury** is a poison, because it is taken by children and men in great quantities without harm. Platter <note>Felix Platter (1536–1614), a Swiss physician who pioneered psychiatric classification</note> reported that it was once drunk by someone indiscriminately, as if it were water; and they record that it is an immediate remedy in cases of **iliac passion** <term>iliac passion: a historical term for a painful and often fatal intestinal obstruction</term>. See Aegineta <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician whose encyclopedia was a standard medical text</note>, *Book 7, on Mercury*.

Why, therefore, do they not dread the "poison" of mercury when it is found in iron and steel? It is in no way different from common **mercury**, except for the clinging of certain impurities. For mercury, in itself and by its very essence, is quite beneficial—an observation confirmed by the evidence of practical experience. If it contains anything poisonous...

### IV.

It increases febrile heat, according to the witness of Actuarius <note>Joannes Actuarius (c. 1275–1328), a prominent Byzantine physician whose works were widely studied in the Renaissance</note> in Book 6 of his *Method of Healing*, chapter 5, because of the extraordinary acrimony <note>original: "acrimoniam"; referring to a sharp, biting, or caustic quality</note> which it possesses.

### V.

It is to be condemned because we use it without relying on the authority of any proven authors <note>The author is highlighting the "unorthodox" nature of chemical medicine, which lacked the thousand-year pedigree of Greek herbalism</note>.

### VI.

Galen, in Book 10 of his *Method of Healing*, chapter 2, and in chapter 9 of the 11th book of the same work, held water of vitriol <note>original: "calcanthinam aquam"; a solution made from vitriol</note> as suspect in cases of putrid fevers <note>Putrid fevers were thought to be caused by the "rotting" of the body's humors</note>, since when applied to the skin, it is not only prone to causing a constriction of the pores, but it also imparts excessive heat to the body.

### VII.

Safer remedies are held to exist for resisting putrefaction than <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "calcantho"; vitriol is a sulfate mineral, usually of iron or copper, used in early chemistry</note> itself.

### IIX.

The oil, once the earthy parts have been removed through distillation, acquires more fire <note>Distillation was seen as a way of concentrating the "fiery" essence of a mineral; the critics argue this makes it too dangerous for a feverish patient</note> than the <term>vitriol</term> itself.

### IX.

Just as poison exists in all metals, so too it is present in <term>vitriol</term>, which is ruinous in cases of malignant fevers <note>Malignant fevers were those considered particularly deadly or contagious, often accompanied by spots or extreme weakness</note>.

On the contrary, the latter is fought by the former. Therefore, there is no fear to be had from its burning heat. I would not call it a simple or burning heat. The quality of a mixture is itself mixed; it is not to be determined by the concept of heat alone. 

However, the very sharp oil of vitriol is not used for curing fevers; rather, the **spirit** or the acidic oil of vitriol is used instead. You cannot deny that it possesses the power to blunt <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the supposed "rotting" of bodily fluids thought to cause disease</note> and extinguish febrile heat, nor can you claim that an internal fire dwells within it. One might as well take away or attribute the same properties to all acidic vegetables, which are nevertheless used most frequently in the treatment of fevers.

That a wonderful power exists in the spirit of vitriol, as well as in the **acid of sulfur**, to quench febrile heats and unnatural burnings and inflammations, is clear from this evidence: although it is drawn out from combustible **sulfur**, it is so far from being prone to catching fire that it even prevents **gunpowder** <note>original: "pulvis pyrius"</note> from being ignited...

### IV. Refutation <note>original: *Lysis*; Greek for a solution or the dismantling of an argument</note>

In their fourth argument, they **beg the question** <term>original: *petunt principium*; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed to be true in the premises</term> with a shameful and empty rebuttal. To reveal the falsehood more clearly, let the **reasoning** <note>original: *dianoia*; Greek for the process of thought or discursive intellect</note> be structured as a formal **syllogism** <term>a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term>:

*Whatever is analogous to the **innate heat** <term>the *calor nativus*, the vital warmth believed to be the primary tool of the soul</term>, and is also incorruptible and contrary to all diseases, that is a **universal medicine** <note>original: *catholica medicina*</note>. The **Philosophers' Stone** is similar to the innate heat, incorruptible, and contrary to all diseases.*

Therefore [the Stone is a universal medicine]. This connection is denied. For how can something that is incorruptible be similar to the innate heat? Innate heat is corruptible; at every moment it exhales through **imperceptible perspiration** <note>original: *atheōrēton diapnoēn*; a Greek medical term for the invisible evaporation of vital vapors through the pores</note>, existing in a state of constant regeneration. What similarity, therefore, is there between [this heat and the Stone]?

# Preliminary Exercises

Once the **innate heat** <term>the *calor nativus*, or the body's internal vital fire</term> has been restored, every enemy [disease] will be put to flight; nevertheless, a **universal medicine** cannot exist for that reason. ## QUESTION LII.

->*Whether similar or contrary remedies should be sought out: that is, whether likes are cured by likes, or indeed contraries by contraries?*<-

It is a maxim and precept of the **Chemists** <term>Chymicorum; here referring to the Paracelsians or "Spagyrists" who used minerals and chemical processes</term> that *likes are cured by likes* <note>original: *similia curari similibus*, the foundation of what would later be called homeopathy</note>. That of the **Galenists** <term>Galenicorum; followers of the traditional Greek medical system based on the four humors</term> is diametrically opposed: that *contraries are cured by contraries* <note>original: *contraria contrariis curari*</note> according to the law of **opposition** <note>original Greek: τῆς ὑπεναντίωσις (*tēs hypenantiōsis*)</note> established by Hippocrates. It is rightly asked **whether these pronouncements contradict one another.** Indeed, so fierce has been the war between the Chemists and the Galenists that, because of this single controversy, it has been thought until now that they could in no way ever agree with one another for all eternity. But it is answered that there is no contradiction, because neither statement differs **in the same respect** <note>original Greek: πρὸς ταυτὸ (*pros tauto*)</note> if they are understood fairly. The Chemists maintain that likes are cured by likes, and they are indeed so cured. By what argument? It is nature itself that opposes the disease by putting it to flight. Hence Hippocrates, in his fifth commentary on the sixth book of *Epidemics*, says: **Natures are the physicians of diseases.** <note>original Greek: φύσιες ἰητροὶ τῶν νόσων (*physies iētroi tōn nosōn*)</note> From which Galen, in the first book of *On the Regimen of Diet in Acute Diseases*...

-> # Preliminary Exercises <-

**Galen**, in the first book of *On the Natural Faculties*, drawing from **Hippocrates** when describing the power of nature, says that in our bodies there is "one conspiracy and one conflux" <note>original: *unum conspiratum confluxumque*; a classical medical concept suggesting that all parts of the body breathe together in total harmony and functional unity</note>: which Hippocrates set forth in his book *On Food*, and also in the *Epidemics*, Book 6, Section 6. He stated that nature is just and alone sufficient for living creatures; that she acts by herself, without a teacher, doing what is necessary. From this, he concludes that she possesses certain **faculties** <term>natural powers or functions inherent in an organ or organism</term>: one by which she attracts what is suitable to her, and another by which she expels what is foreign from herself. 

This is also consistent with the common consensus of physicians—not to mention Hippocrates himself—who assert that some medicines purge **yellow bile**, others **black bile**, others **phlegm** <term>pituita; the cold, moist humor</term>, and others watery and thin waste. Indeed, Hippocrates himself confirmed this in so many words in his book *On the Nature of Man*. Therefore, Galen attributes a significant **attractive power** <note>original: *vim attractoriam*</note> to medicines, by which they draw to themselves the humors that are "familiar" to them. 

Hence, **scammony** <note>a resin from the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*, used as a powerful purgative</note> is said to draw bile, **safflower** <note>carthamus</note> phlegm, **dodder of thyme** <note>epithymum</note> black bile, and **sea cabbage** <note>brassica marina</note> watery and serous humors, by a certain analogy, familiarity, and similarity of substance.

### Alchemy, Question 52

...they are said to be the same: yet nonetheless, they have also medicated through **contraries** <note>original: contraria</note>, because by clearing and removing **obstructions** <term>obstructions; in Galenic medicine, blockages in the vessels or organs that prevent the flow of humors</term>, they restore health once the causes of the obstruction have been led out. In this way, a cure may be achieved through contraries by considering not only the disease itself but also its causes. Thus, by removing obstructions with hot remedies, we remove the fever, always holding health and disease as opposing subjects; we resist disease by curing with contraries, and even by those applied in a contrary manner. 

For **contraries** are understood in many ways. Some are called simple contraries, such as **hot** versus **cold**; others are privative <note>opposites defined by the absence of a quality</note>, such as **full** versus **empty**, **continuous** versus **solid** <note>referring to the physical integrity or "oneness" of a body part versus its disruption</note>, or **whole** versus **corrupt**. 

Some are contrary to the disease in their own right <note>Latin: per se</note>, while others are so by accident <note>Latin: per accidens</note>. Things opposed to the disease in their own right include: **hot** for **cold**, something that calms and repels agitation, something that evacuates excess, something that thickens thinness, something that softens hardness, something that cleanses stickiness, or applying a sticky substance to sharp acidity; something that strengthens laxity, **antidotes** <term>alexiteria; medicines that ward off poison or the effects of corruption</term> against corruption, and things that promote "ripening" <note>concoction; the process of maturing or "cooking" humors to make them easier for the body to expel</note>, the formation of pus, and purging for putrefaction and roughness...

### [Of the Preliminary Exercises]

...smoothing what is rough, dilating narrowness, thinning what is dense, opening what is blocked, and bonding together a broken continuity <note>original: solutioni continuae; a classical medical term for a wound or fracture where the physical integrity of the body is "dissolved"</note> with a flesh-making <term>sarcotic; a substance that encourages the growth of new tissue in a wound</term> or scar-forming <term>epulotic; a medication that dries a wound to facilitate scarring</term> remedy. 

Some things are contrary in act <note>meaning they currently possess an active quality, like heat</note>, others in potentiality <note>meaning they have the power to become active under certain conditions</note>, or by both power and act. 

In a few words, the nature of "contrariety" is explained thus: namely, by the removal of that which is in excess and the addition of that which is lacking. As **Hippocrates** rightly stated elsewhere, medicine is nothing other than the addition of what is deficient and the subtraction of what is redundant. Since things can be redundant or deficient in both quantity and quality, individual treatments are carried out through contraries in both respects. 

Chemical physicians <term>chymiatri; early modern practitioners who integrated alchemical chemistry into medical practice</term> satisfy this whole principle of contrariety, even though they may heal using "likes." Because by administering specific and similar remedies, they remove either the disease or its cause, and thus it must be held that they have cured through contraries. Indeed, while the chemists <note>chymici</note> assert that "likes are cured by likes," or rather <note>catchword: potius</note> that similar remedies should be sought, they actually confirm the Method of **Galen** and **Hippocrates’** principle of opposition <note>original Greek: tēs hupenantiōseōs; the fundamental medical law that diseases are cured by their opposites</note>.

<summary>This page argues that alchemical medicine, which uses "likes" to treat "likes," does not actually contradict the traditional Greek medical law of "contraries," because the end result is still the removal of excess or the filling of deficiency.</summary>

## QUESTION LIII.

### *Whether potable gold <note>original: aurum potabile; gold rendered into a liquid form for medicinal ingestion</note> can be made, and whether it has any use for the preservation and extension of human life?*

Those who deny that gold can be made drinkable rely on the opposing testimony of certain chemists <note>original: chymicorum</note>, as well as on the difficulty of its preparation. For they argue that it requires many boilings <note>original: coctiones; a standard alchemical process of heating substances over long periods</note>, by which the original moisture <note>the "radical moisture" believed to give metals their flexibility and life</note> of the gold is completely drained away, and its body is reduced to a withered state of wasting <note>original: atrophiam</note> and an extremely arid powder <note>original: calcem; "calx" refers to the crumbly ash or powder left after a metal has been burned or calcined</note>; they claim this does not happen even with gold leaf.

But it is answered: It cannot be denied by any who are truly chemists that gold can be made drinkable, since they themselves have taught the methods for extracting the essence of gold through a unique **solvent** <term>menstruum: a specialized liquid used in alchemy to dissolve solid bodies, named after the lunar cycle</term>. If it cannot be dissolved, what is the point of establishing a rule for the dissolution of gold? And if other metals are dissolved, then gold also will be subject to **dissolution** <note>original: solutioni</note>. But the former is truer than true <note>a logical idiom meaning "self-evidently true"</note>. Therefore, so is the latter. The very difficulty of the preparation or dissolution confirms its possibility rather than denies it.

**Alchemy, potable gold, chemist, medicine, preparation, dissolution.**

It is established, therefore, that even when heterogeneous things are brought into a union that appears **homogeneous** <term>homogeneous: appearing uniform or consistent throughout</term> to the senses, a **harmonious discord** <note>original: concors discordia; the idea that a stable substance is actually a balance of opposing forces</note> and a **hostile friendship** <gloss>original Greek: φιλέχθρα (philechthra): a paradoxical term for the attraction and repulsion between different elements</gloss> emerge. Through the art of separation, every metal and mineral naturally gives way into distinct heterogeneous parts: **mercurial**, **sulfurous**, and **salty** <note>These are the "Tria Prima" or three primary principles of Paracelsian alchemy: Mercury (spirit/liquidity), Sulfur (soul/combustibility), and Salt (body/solidity)</note>, as well as other heterogeneous dross. How, then, can metals be homogeneous?

Alchemy, Question 56.

If natural fire is considered natural because it claims an internal principle of motion, why should it not, on the contrary, be judged artificial when it claims an industrious external governor of its motion? Unless you deny that opposite things have opposite definitions. Therefore, fire can be both natural and artificial, conditioned in different ways and consequently to be viewed in different ways.

While that potentiality <term>potentia: the inherent capacity to become something more</term> might be perfected by the passage of time, [the Art] requires it to be actualized immediately. Thus, it is vain to seek the **seminal virtue of the stone** in imperfect things, when the most perfect substances are available for the most perfect [works].
